props.title: The Orphanage

sections.content: The Orphanage (2007) stands as one of the most haunting Spanish horror films, produced by Guillermo del Toro and directed by J.A. Bayona in his feature debut. Like del Toro's Pan's Labyrinth (2006), it masterfully blends childhood trauma with supernatural elements. The film follows Laura, who returns to her childhood orphanage to open a home for disabled children, only to face increasingly disturbing events when her adopted son Simón disappears. It draws from classic ghost stories like The Innocents (1961) and The Others (2001), using children's games and empty corridors to build unbearable tension rather than relying on cheap jump scares.

sections.content: The film's brilliance lies in its dual nature as both ghost story and meditation on maternal grief. Like Don't Look Now (1973), it uses supernatural elements to explore the psychology of loss. Bayona creates a rich visual language drawing from Spanish Gothic architecture and Victorian ghost photography, while Belén Rueda's devastating performance as Laura anchors the supernatural elements in raw emotional truth. The film established a template for sophisticated horror that influenced later works like Mama (2013) and The Babadook (2014).

Bayona's attention to period detail and use of practical effects creates a timeless quality similar to The Haunting (1963). The orphanage itself becomes a character, with its creaking floorboards and shadowy corners hiding both literal and metaphorical ghosts. The film's approach to childhood trauma echoes through later Spanish horror like Marrowbone (2017) and Veronica (2017), proving influential in elevating supernatural horror beyond simple scares. sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond Spanish cinema, helping establish a new wave of emotionally resonant horror typified by films like A Tale of Two Sisters (2003) and The Woman in Black (2012). Its success proved audiences would embrace slow-burn supernatural stories that prioritize atmosphere and emotional depth over conventional horror tropes. This paved the way for sophisticated ghost stories like Under the Shadow (2016) and I Am the Pretty Thing That Lives in the House (2016).
